notes.meaning: Paul addresses shocking news that had reached him about gross sexual sin in Corinth. A man in the congregation was living in a sexual relationship with his stepmother. Even the surrounding non-Christian Roman society viewed such behavior as shameful and illegal. Paul wanted this dealt with because it brought dishonor to the church.

The Corinthian Christians were proud of themselves instead of feeling brokenhearted over this sin. They should have grieved deeply and removed the unrepentant man from their church family. Excommunication, which means taking away a person's membership in church fellowship, was needed to protect the congregation. Christians must never confuse tolerating blatant sin with Christian love.

Even though Paul was physically away from Corinth, his heart and thoughts were right there with them. Speaking with the authority Jesus gave him as an apostle, he had already reached a clear decision about the case. He judged the offender just as if he were present in person. True spiritual leaders do not ignore open rebellion against God's commands.

Paul tells the congregation to gather together formally in the name and authority of the Lord Jesus. His own spiritual authority and the power of Jesus would be with them in that meeting. Church discipline was not meant to be done by one person acting in secret. It was to be a unified, public act carried out under Christ's direction.

The church was ordered to put the man out of their fellowship, placing him back into the realm of Satan outside God's household. Removing him was meant to break his sinful desires through painful consequences. The goal of this discipline was not to destroy him forever, but to bring him to repentance so he would be saved when Jesus returns.

differ.view: Being handed over to Satan simply means being put out of the church. The 'flesh' destroyed is his sinful nature, tamed so he may live for God.
Satan was usually allowed to bring pain or sickness on such an offender, unless he quickly repented.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church teachers and Catholic theology understand this as expelling the sinner from the church and its sacraments, leaving him vulnerable to physical affliction or Satan's buffetings so that bodily suffering might awaken his conscience before the final judgment.

notes.meaning: The Corinthians had no right to boast about their gifts while allowing such corruption to continue. Paul quotes a common proverb about how a tiny bit of yeast spreads through an entire lump of dough. In the same way, leaving one member's open sin uncorrected will slowly infect the whole congregation. Sin always spreads if it is ignored.

Paul commands them to clean out the old yeast of sin so the church can be pure and fresh. Just as Jewish homes cleared away all yeast before the Passover feast, believers must clear away unrepentant sin. Christ has already died as the true Passover Lamb who takes away our guilt. Since Jesus made believers clean, their daily lives should match that reality.

Christians are called to live their entire lives as an ongoing celebration of God's goodness. That feast must not be tainted with the old yeast of bitter hatred and evil deeds. Instead, believers are to feed on Christ by walking in total honesty, sincerity, and truth.

Paul mentions an earlier letter he had written that told the Corinthians not to mingle with sexually immoral people. That earlier letter was not kept as part of the Bible, and some readers had misunderstood what he meant. Paul wanted to make sure they knew how to apply his warning properly in their daily lives.

Paul explains that he never meant they should cut off contact with everyday unbelievers who are greedy, dishonest, or worship false gods. To avoid every sinner in the world, Christians would have to leave the earth completely. God expects His people to interact with the world around them while refusing to copy its corrupt ways.

Paul clarifies that believers must refuse close friendship with anyone who claims to be a Christian brother while persisting in scandalous sins. These include drunkenness, verbal abuse, greed, idolatry, and sexual immorality. Refusing even to eat meals with such a person shows the seriousness of their hypocrisy and urges them to turn back to God.

Paul explains that disciplining people outside the Christian faith is none of his business. The church has no authority to judge or regulate non-Christians. Instead, local congregations are responsible for holding their own members accountable to God's standard.

God Himself will hold outsiders accountable and judge them in His own time. Paul quotes the Old Testament law to give a direct command: the church must expel the wicked person from among them. Putting the unrepentant offender out preserves the purity of God's house and leaves no doubt about what He requires.
